definition.text: A way of buying or selling something by inviting bids and then dealing with the highest (or, when buying, the lowest) bidder.

facts.text: The open ascending-price auction, where each bid must beat the one before, is probably the most common kind and has a long history.
Auctions are used to trade antiques, livestock, radio spectrum, used cars, real estate, online advertising and emission permits, among much else.
Each year the US EPA auctions about 250,000 allowances, each letting its owner emit one ton of sulfur dioxide, to the highest bidders.
Governments earn the most from spectrum auctions and quota auctions; Russia's crab quota sold for €2 billion in 2019.
The branch of economics that studies auction formats and how bidders behave is called auction theory.
Paul Milgrom and Robert B. Wilson won the 2020 Nobel Prize for introducing new auction formats.
Fishing quotas can be handed out for free or auctioned when a catch-share scheme starts.

definition.text: The main ways an auction's price can be set: open rising bids, a falling price called out by the auctioneer, or one-shot sealed bids.

facts.text: In an English auction bidders openly outbid one another, each bid higher than the last.
In a Dutch auction the auctioneer starts high and lowers the price until someone accepts it or the seller's reserve is reached.
In a first-price sealed-bid auction everyone submits one secret bid at the same time and the highest bidder pays what they bid.
A Vickrey (second-price sealed-bid) auction works the same way except that the winner pays the second-highest bid; it is central to auction theory and online ad bidding.

definition.text: A minimum price set by the seller below which the auctioned item will not be sold.

facts.text: In a no-reserve (absolute) auction the item sells whatever the price, which can draw more bidders hoping for a bargain.
A reserve protects the seller from a low bid but may lower the final price if it dampens interest.
The reserve can be announced to bidders (public) or kept secret.

title: Winner's curse

definition.text: The tendency of an auction winner who knows less about an item than the seller to overvalue it and overpay.

facts.text: Bid shading, bidding below one's true value for the item, is one way bidders guard against the winner's curse.
Bid shading risks losing the auction but may win the item cheaply.
When items go to whoever overvalues them most, resources may not end up with the person who values them most.

notes: No page of its own here; drawn from Auction § Bidding strategy > By the bidders.

definition.text: Collusion in which bidders who know each other form a ring to avoid bidding against one another and so keep auction prices low.

facts.text: Ring members may hold their own private auction afterwards and split the price difference between the two sales.
Bid rigging weakens competition, discourages other bidders and denies the seller the item's true value.
Even without explicit agreement, bidders can in theory coordinate tacitly to keep bids low.

definition.text: A game-theory model of strategic decisions in which players have incomplete information, such as private knowledge of their own payoffs.

facts.text: John C. Harsanyi introduced Bayesian games in three papers in 1967 and 1968 and later shared the 1994 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences.
Nature assigns each player a 'type' at the start, standing for the private information that player holds.
Players hold a probability distribution over everyone's possible types; when no one has private information it is called a common prior.
Attaching probabilities to types lets games of incomplete information be solved for the first time, and far more easily than otherwise.
They avoid endless 'I think that you think' reasoning by weighting all possible outcomes by probability at once.
A buyer bidding for a used car whose quality only the owner knows, the market for lemons, is a Bayesian game linked to adverse selection.

definition.text: The Nash equilibrium of a Bayesian game, in which each player's strategy maximizes their expected payoff given their beliefs about others' types and the others' strategies.

facts.text: Players form their beliefs about the unknown state of nature using Bayes' rule.
In dynamic games where players move in turn, it can produce implausible equilibria based on non-credible strategies or beliefs.
In mechanism design, a Bayesian Nash equilibrium in which everyone reports their true preferences makes a mechanism incentive compatible.

definition.text: An equilibrium of a sequential game with incomplete information in which beliefs are consistent with the strategies and every player chooses optimally given those beliefs.

facts.text: Like subgame perfect equilibrium, it requires play to be optimal from every information set onward, ruling out non-credible threats and beliefs.

definition.text: A group of a player's decision points that the player cannot tell apart, so they do not know which one they are at.

facts.text: In game trees information sets are usually drawn with dotted lines.
Chance moves are made by 'Nature', usually shown as an unfilled circle at the root of the tree.
